messages.author: ffe9baa355bd96e5
messages.subject: Bounded ordered vector?
parts:
Hi Everyone, 

I am trying to fit a mixed model with binomial distributions with 3 different probabilities and I want to force that q < pmin < pmax.  I have used the ordered vector to define the parameters but it seems like I cannot define them to be between 0 and 1 directly. I've tried transforming them as follows (just pasting the relevant part of the code below), but I was wondering if there is a better way of doing this:

parameters{
  ordered [3]  rates;
  ...
}

transformed parameters {
real <lower=0, upper=1> q;
real <lower=0, upper=1> pmin;
real <lower=0, upper=1> pmax;

q = inv_logit(rates [1]);
pmin = inv_logit(rates[2]);
pmax = inv_logit(rates[3]);

 ...

}

Thanks a lot!

C

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bounded ordered vector?
parts:
It's fewer lines of code and variables if you do this

parameters {
ordered[3] qp_log_odds;
...
}
transformed parmaeters {
vector[3]<lower=0, upper=1> qp = inv_logit(qplog_odds);

and then just use qp[1], qp[2], and qp[3] instead
of q, pmin, and pmax.

There's also the issue of what's going on in the model.
Setting things up this way requires a Jacobian adjustment
if you want to put a prior on qp rather than on qp_log_odds.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bounded ordered vector?
parts:
Yes, it depends on how they're used on the model.
The Jacobian is just the usual adjustment for a multivariate
change of variables. See the manual chapters

20. Reparameterization & Change of Variables

and then for all of our built-in constraints, we have derivations:

33. Transformations of Constrained Variables

You can also look up changes of variables on Wikipedia or
in any multivariate calc book to get more examples of Jacobians
and why they're needed (just remember that densities are
derivatives of cumulative distribution functions).

- Bob
